512.title: Rahula awakens
512.hook: the Buddha teaches the six senses as not-self, and Rahula awakens
512.howItsDone: Theravada teachers use this discourse's three questions as a pattern for insight practice: is it permanent, is it unsatisfactory, is it fit to be called self?

segments.voice: Yesterday: Nandaka teaching the nuns, and your line, the moon is full. Did you teach one thing kindly? Today the Buddha takes his own son into the forest. Day five hundred twelve.

We've met Rahula before in this collection: a boy taught with a mirror, then a young monk told to be like the earth and like water. Now, in the hundred and forty-seventh discourse, he's grown. One day near Savatthi, the Buddha reflects that the qualities that ripen into freedom have ripened in Rahula. So after the alms round he says: Rahula, bring your sitting cloth. We'll spend the day in the Dark Forest. A father and a son walk out of the city and sit down under a tree. The text adds that many thousands of gods followed them, wanting to hear. Today: Rahula awakens.
screen: `THE BOY WITH THE MIRROR, GROWN.` → `BRING YOUR SITTING CLOTH.` → `UNDER A TREE IN THE DARK FOREST.`

segments.voice: The teaching is a string of questions, and Rahula answers every one himself. Rahula, is the eye permanent or impermanent? Impermanent, venerable sir. And what is impermanent, is it suffering or ease? Suffering. And what is impermanent, suffering, bound to change: is it fit to be seen as, this is mine, this I am, this is my self? No, venerable sir. Then the same three questions again, for forms, the things the eye sees. For eye-consciousness, the seeing itself. For eye-contact, the meeting of eye and form. For the feeling, perception, choices and awareness that come out of that meeting. Then all of it over again, for the ear, the nose, the tongue, the body and the mind. Notice the method. The Buddha doesn't announce a doctrine and ask Rahula to accept it. He asks, and lets his son look and say what he sees. The Pali word under every answer is anicca: impermanent, changing. Not only the world out there, but the instrument doing the looking, and the looking itself. Then the conclusion. Seeing this, the Buddha says, a noble disciple grows disenchanted with the eye, with forms, with seeing, and becomes dispassionate, and through dispassion the mind is freed. While he was speaking, the text says, Rahula's mind was freed from the taints, through not clinging. And the gods who had followed saw something too: whatever has the nature to arise, all of that has the nature to cease. In the Vinaya's story of his going forth, the boy Rahula asks his father for his inheritance. Here, under a tree, he receives it, as questions.
screen: `IS THE EYE PERMANENT?` · `FORMS, SEEING, CONTACT, FEELING` · `SIX SENSES, THE SAME QUESTIONS` · `RAHULA'S MIND IS FREED` · then, large: `ALL OF IT CHANGING.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: watch the senses. Keep your eyes open for a moment. Notice something you're seeing, and notice the seeing itself shifting: light, focus, a blink. Now close your eyes. A sound arrives and fades. A touch: the chair under you, air on your hands, changing even while you notice it. Each time something arises, you can say quietly, changing. Not as a sad word. Just as a true one. The bell holds the time.
Rahula awakens. Anicca, impermanence, seen in the senses themselves: the eye, what it sees, and the seeing. Today's word.
Your line: all of it changing. Today, when one sight or sound grabs you, notice that the eye and ear doing the grabbing are changing too. Day five hundred twelve.

pairs: where father and son spent the day
the meeting of eye and form

it's a string of questions, and Rahula answers every one himself.
the questions cover not just the eye but the seeing and the contact too
forms, eye-consciousness, eye-contact and what arises from it, then all six senses.
the text says many gods followed them to the forest
and while Rahula was freed, they saw that whatever arises has the nature to cease.

fork.setup: you're Rahula, under the tree. the Buddha asks: what is impermanent and bound to change, is it fit to be seen as 'this is my self'? what do you say?
options: no, venerable sir.
yes, if it's my own eye.
only the mind is my self.
fork.reveal: Rahula answers no, every time, for every sense. the Buddha lets him see it for himself instead of telling him.

original.note: Pali anicca: impermanent, changing. Sanskrit anitya. here, the eye, what it sees, and the seeing itself.

trapdoor: what you thought: Rahula awakens means he woke up one morning enlightened.
what it means: his mind is freed from the taints while his father questions him about the six senses.
what a scholar hears: the same teaching appears in the Samyutta Nikaya's book on the six senses, and some readers see it as the ripening of years of training that began with the mirror talk in MN 61.

513.title: Six sets of six
513.hook: the eye is not self, forms are not self, seeing is not self
513.howItsDone: The six sense bases are a standard frame for insight meditation in Theravada practice; teachers often walk students through them one at a time, asking whether anything found there is lasting or can be called self.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Rahula awakens under a tree, and your line, all of it changing. Did you catch the eye changing while it looked? Today the same senses, counted out like beads. Day five hundred thirteen.

Thirty-six. That's how many items the hundred and forty-eighth discourse lays out, in six rows of six, like a spreadsheet of experience. It opens in Jeta's Grove at Savatthi with the Buddha announcing a teaching good in the beginning, good in the middle, good in the end. Then he simply counts. It can sound dry on the page, almost like an inventory. But the text itself says that while it was being spoken, the minds of sixty monks were freed. Today: six sets of six.
screen: `THIRTY-SIX ITEMS, SIX ROWS OF SIX.` → `JETA'S GROVE, SAVATTHI.` → `SIXTY MONKS FREED.`

segments.voice: Here are the six rows. First, the six inner bases: eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, mind. Second, the six outer bases: forms, sounds, smells, tastes, touches, and things known by the mind. Third, six kinds of consciousness, one for each meeting: seeing, hearing, and so on. Fourth, six kinds of contact, when sense, object and consciousness come together. Fifth, six kinds of feeling born of that contact. Sixth, six kinds of craving born of that feeling. Then comes the argument, and it's short. If anyone says the eye is self, the Buddha says, that doesn't hold. Why? Because the eye's arising and passing away are plainly seen. And if the eye were self, you'd have to say: my self arises and passes away. So the eye is not self. Then he runs the same test down the whole table. Forms: not self. Eye-consciousness: not self. Eye-contact, feeling, craving: not self. Thirty-six times, the same short proof. The Pali word is anatta, not-self. Notice what it doesn't say. It doesn't say nobody is here, or that nothing matters. It says that each piece you might point to and call me is something that comes and goes, so it can't be the permanent owner you were looking for. Then the discourse turns practical. When a pleasant feeling comes and you delight in it, a tendency toward lust is lying underneath. A painful one, and you resist it, aversion lies underneath. A neutral one, unnoticed, and ignorance lies underneath. Seeing all six rows clearly, the text says, a person grows disenchanted, and is freed.
screen: `SIX INNER, SIX OUTER` · `CONSCIOUSNESS, CONTACT, FEELING, CRAVING` · `IF THE EYE WERE SELF…` · `WHAT LIES UNDERNEATH A FEELING` · then, large: `NOT SELF, SIX TIMES.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: check one sense for a self. Choose hearing. Close your eyes and let sounds come. A car. Your own breath. A hum. Now look for the one who owns the hearing. There's the sound. There's the ear. There's the hearing, arising and fading. Is there anything else, standing apart and permanent? Don't argue with yourself. Just look, and keep looking, gently. The bell holds the time.
Six sets of six. Thirty-six pieces of experience, each one arising and passing, so none of them the lasting self. Anatta, tested row by row. Today's word.
Your line: not self, six times. Today, when a feeling seems to be all of you, notice it arrived through one of six doors, and it will leave. Day five hundred thirteen.

the text says sixty monks were freed while it was spoken
the discourse closes by saying so: sixty monks freed from the taints, through not clinging.
the argument is: if the eye were self, my self would arise and pass away
since the eye's arising and passing is plain to see, the eye isn't self.

fork.setup: someone tells you: the eye is my self. what does the Buddha in MN 148 point to?
options: the eye arises and passes away, so the self would too.
the eye is too small to be a self.
only the mind can be a self.
fork.reveal: he points to change: if the eye were self, you'd have to say 'my self arises and passes away', and that doesn't hold.

original.note: Pali anatta: not-self. Sanskrit anatman. tested here on thirty-six pieces of experience.

trapdoor: what you thought: not-self means you don't exist.
what it means: every piece of experience you could call 'me' arises and passes, so none is the lasting owner.
what a scholar hears: the argument works by consequence (if the eye were self, the self would arise and pass), and later Buddhist schools debated at length what the conventional person is.

sources.ref: Majjhima Nikaya 148, Chachakka Sutta (the six sets of six)

514.title: Not inflamed
514.hook: not knowing the eye as it is, one is inflamed; knowing it, one is free
514.howItsDone: Theravada meditators practice sense restraint and bare noticing, seeing what comes through each sense as it actually is; teachers often pair this with calm practice so that, as MN 149 says, calm and insight develop together.

segments.voice: Yesterday: six sets of six, and your line, not self, six times. Did a feeling arrive through one door and leave again? Today, what happens when we don't see those doors clearly. Day five hundred fourteen.

A bakery window at the end of a long day. Glazed pastries under warm light, a cake with a perfect swirl. The glass hasn't changed since morning, and the person walking past hadn't wanted cake a minute ago. Now there's heat, a pull, a little restlessness. The hundred and forty-ninth discourse has a word for that state. The Pali is saratta, usually rendered inflamed, or impassioned. And it says the fire doesn't start in the cake or the window. It starts in how things are seen. Today: not inflamed.
screen: `A BAKERY WINDOW, LATE.` → `A SUDDEN PULL.` → `SARATTA: INFLAMED.`

segments.voice: The discourse is called the great six sense bases, and it begins with a contrast. When someone doesn't know and see the eye as it actually is, the Buddha says, and doesn't know forms, eye-consciousness, eye-contact and the feeling that comes from it as they actually are, they become inflamed by lust for all of it. Inflamed, tied up, infatuated, fixed on the sweetness. And then things build. Craving grows. The heaps of clinging pile up for the future. Troubles of body and mind grow, torments grow, fevers grow. And the person feels it, in the body and in the mind. Now the other side. When someone knows and sees the eye as it actually is, and the forms, and the seeing, they aren't inflamed. Craving fades. The heaps of clinging shrink. The fevers go down. And the text says this person feels ease, in body and in mind. The key phrase is yathabhuta: as it actually is. Not as advertised, not as feared. Just as it is. Notice what's not being blamed. Not the eye. Not the world. The eye is fine. The cake is fine. The problem is the fog between them. And then a surprise. For a person who sees this way, the text says, their view simply is right view, their intention right intention, their effort right effort. The eightfold path, the text says, comes to fulfillment in them. Calm and insight, it says, run together, evenly yoked. Like two oxen under one yoke, pulling one cart.
screen: `NOT SEEING CLEARLY: INFLAMED` · `CRAVING GROWS, FEVERS GROW` · `SEEING AS IT ACTUALLY IS` · `THE PATH FULFILLS ITSELF` · then, large: `NOT INFLAMED.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: know one sense clearly. Rest one hand on something near you: a sleeve, a table, your own knee. First just texture and temperature. Then notice whether there's a small liking or disliking, a pull toward it or away. Don't fix it. Just name it: liking, or not liking, or neither. Now let the hand go still and rest with whatever's left of the touch. Notice the temperature of the mind. Is it warm, cool, still? The bell holds the time.
Not inflamed. Seeing the senses as they actually are, yathabhuta, so the pull of what's seen doesn't set the mind on fire. Today's word.
Your line: not inflamed. Today, when something in a window or on a screen pulls at you, pause and see it as it is: light, color, a little wanting. Day five hundred fourteen.

myth: MN 149 says the eye itself is the problem
the eye is fine. the problem is not knowing it, and what it sees, as it actually is.
the text says clear seeing brings ease in body and mind
fevers and torments go down, and the person feels ease.
for someone who sees clearly, the eightfold path is said to come to fulfillment
their view simply is right view, their effort right effort, and so on.

fork.setup: a beautiful thing catches your eye and the old heat starts to rise. what does MN 149 point to?
options: see the eye, the thing and the feeling as they actually are.
never look at anything beautiful again.
get the thing quickly so the heat stops.
fork.reveal: the discourse doesn't ask anyone to close their eyes. it asks them to see clearly, and says the inflaming fades when they do.

original.note: Pali yathabhuta: as it actually is, as it has come to be. the key to not being inflamed.

trapdoor: what you thought: not inflamed means not getting angry.
what it means: not set on fire by craving for what the senses bring.
what a scholar hears: MN 149 links clear seeing of the six bases directly to the eightfold path and to calm and insight 'yoked evenly', a key text for how the two kinds of meditation fit together.

sources.ref: Majjhima Nikaya 149, Mahasalayatanika Sutta (the great discourse on the six sense bases)

515.title: Who deserves respect
515.hook: teachers free of greed, hate and delusion deserve respect
515.howItsDone: In Buddhist communities respect for teachers is shown through bowing, offerings and service; the discourses also encourage lay people to watch a teacher's conduct over time, as in MN 150 and MN 47, before placing trust.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the fog between the eye and the world, and your line, not inflamed. Did something on a screen pull, and did you see it as it was? Today, a village asks a practical question. Day five hundred fifteen.

How do you decide whose advice to trust? Follower counts? A title? A confident voice? In the hundred and fiftieth discourse, the Buddha is walking through Kosala with a large company of monks and stops at a brahmin village called Nagaravinda. The householders come out to meet him. Some bow. Some just exchange polite greetings. Some sit down in silence. And he gives them a question to be ready for, because wanderers from other groups may well ask it. Today: who deserves respect.
screen: `WHOSE ADVICE DO YOU TRUST?` → `A BRAHMIN VILLAGE, NAGARAVINDA.` → `A QUESTION TO BE READY FOR.`

segments.voice: Suppose, the Buddha says, wanderers of other groups ask you: which recluses and brahmins should not be honored or respected? Here's how to answer. Those who aren't free of greed, hate and delusion for what the eye sees, the ear hears, and the rest. Whose minds aren't at peace inside. Who act well one day and badly the next, in body, speech and mind. Why not honor them? Because we, the householders would say, are like that ourselves. We see nothing higher in them. And which should be honored? Those who are free of greed, hate and delusion toward what the senses bring, whose minds are at peace, who act well steadily, in body, speech and mind. Because we see something higher in them than in ourselves. Notice what's missing from this test. No mention of robes. No mention of which teacher someone follows, or which group. The test makes no exception for the Buddha's own monks. The measure is the same for everyone: what has this person done with greed, hate and delusion. The Pali words are lobha, dosa, moha, the three roots the discourses keep returning to. Then the Buddha supplies the next question those wanderers would ask. How would you know? What's the evidence? And the answer is quietly practical. Look at how they live. Such teachers go to the forest, to remote places, where there are no sights or sounds or tastes to delight in. They choose the quiet. You can see the choice. So respect isn't about rank, and it isn't blind. It's earned by a visible life, and you're allowed to watch before you give it.
screen: `WHICH TEACHERS NOT TO HONOR` · `WHICH TEACHERS TO HONOR` · `THE TEST: GREED, HATE, DELUSION` · `THE EVIDENCE: HOW THEY LIVE` · then, large: `WHO TO RESPECT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: honor one gentle teacher. Bring to mind someone who taught you something without trying to be admired. A grandparent, a coach, a nurse, a friend. Picture how they lived: what they didn't grab, what they didn't hate, what they saw clearly. Let a little gratitude rise. If you like, bow your head slightly, inside or out. The bell holds the time.
Who deserves respect. Not the title or the group, but the one free of greed, hate and delusion, and you can see it in how they live. Today's word.
Your line: who to respect. Today, when someone's confidence impresses you, look one layer down: how do they handle wanting and anger? Day five hundred fifteen.

the test is the same for everyone: freedom from greed, hate and delusion, seen in conduct.

they would say: we see something higher in them than in ourselves.
the evidence offered is the teachers' choice of quiet, remote places
they live where there's nothing for the senses to delight in.

fork.setup: you're a householder in Nagaravinda. wandering teachers ask: which recluses deserve your respect? what does the Buddha tell you to answer?
options: those free of greed, hate and delusion, whose minds are at peace.
those who belong to the Buddha's order.
those with the most followers.
fork.reveal: he gives a test anyone can apply to anyone, including his own monks: what have they done with greed, hate and delusion, and does their life show it?

original.note: Pali lobha, dosa, moha: greed, hate, delusion, the three roots. the measure of a teacher in MN 150.

trapdoor: what you thought: respect goes to whoever holds the title.
what it means: in MN 150, respect is earned by freedom from greed, hate and delusion, visible in how someone lives.
what a scholar hears: the discourse echoes MN 47, where even the Buddha invites investigation, and reflects a world of competing wandering teachers in which lay supporters needed criteria.

sources.ref: Majjhima Nikaya 150, Nagaravindeyya Sutta (to the people of Nagaravinda)

516.title: Reviewing the alms round
516.hook: after the alms walk, ask: did desire arise on the way?
516.howItsDone: In Theravada countries monks still walk an alms round, bowl in hand, and looking back over one's actions, taught here and in the earlier advice to Rahula (MN 61), is part of monastic and lay training.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the village of Nagaravinda, and your line, who to respect. Whose handling of wanting and anger did you notice? Today, a way to check your own. Day five hundred sixteen.

Sariputta comes out of his solitary sitting one evening in the Bamboo Grove at Rajagaha and goes to the Buddha. The Buddha looks at him and says: Sariputta, your faculties are clear. Your face is pure and bright. What have you been abiding in? Emptiness, venerable sir. Good, the Buddha says. That is the abiding of great people. And then, instead of praising the meditation further, he talks about something ordinary: the morning walk into town to collect food. Today: reviewing the alms round.
screen: `EVENING, THE BAMBOO GROVE.` → `YOUR FACE IS CLEAR AND BRIGHT.` → `NOW: THE MORNING WALK.`

segments.voice: A monk who wants to dwell in emptiness, the Buddha says, should look back like this. On the road I took into the village for alms, in the place where I walked collecting food, on the road I took back: was there any desire, lust, hate, delusion or aversion in my mind toward the things I saw? The things I heard, smelled, tasted, touched, thought? If he finds there was, he should make an effort to let it go. If he finds there wasn't, he can live with that gladness, training day and night. That's it. A walk, remembered honestly. The alms round, pindapata, is a walk monks still make today in Theravada countries, bowl in hand, receiving whatever is given. So it's a good test: sights of food, smells from kitchens, people kind and people not. Then the discourse widens the review into a long checklist. Have I let go of the five strands of sense pleasure? The five hindrances? Have I understood the five heaps? Developed the foundations of mindfulness, the factors of awakening, the eightfold path? Calm and insight? Each time, the same two answers: if not yet, keep making effort; if so, rest in that gladness. The title of the discourse means the purification of almsfood. The idea is that a walk reviewed this way makes the food, and the life it supports, clean. What's striking is the tone. No guilt, no punishment. Just an honest look back at the road, and then the next step. Notice too who it's taught to: Sariputta, whose bright face the Buddha has just praised. Even he is told to check.
screen: `DID DESIRE ARISE ON THE WAY?` · `IF SO, LET IT GO; IF NOT, BE GLAD` · `THE LONG CHECKLIST` · `A WALK REVIEWED, A LIFE MADE CLEAN` · then, large: `REVIEW THE ROAD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: review your walk home. Or your last trip anywhere: to the store, the office, the kitchen. Close your eyes and replay it slowly. The door. The street or hallway. What you saw. Did wanting rise somewhere? Irritation? A fog? Where was it, exactly? If you find something, just note it and breathe it out. If you find a stretch that was clear, rest there and be glad. The bell holds the time.
Reviewing the alms round. Looking back honestly at the road you walked: if desire arose, let it go; if not, be glad and keep training. Today's word.
Your line: review the road. Tonight, before sleep, walk back through one trip you made today and see what rose on the way. Day five hundred sixteen.

fork.reveal: the text allows gladness: if the road was clear, rest in that joy and keep training.

original.note: Pali pindapata: almsfood, and the alms round that collects it.

trapdoor: what you thought: the alms round is just how monks get lunch.
what it means: in MN 151 it becomes a practice, reviewed afterward for desire, hate and delusion.
what a scholar hears: the title, Pindapataparisuddhi, means purification of almsfood: the review is how a monastic makes the gift that sustains them well used.

sources.ref: Majjhima Nikaya 151, Pindapataparisuddhi Sutta (the purification of almsfood)

517.title: Seeing, not swept
517.hook: the last discourse: training the senses is not closing the eyes but seeing without being swept away
517.howItsDone: Buddhist meditators in several schools practice open-eyed awareness and sense restraint in daily life: noticing liking and disliking as they arise and returning to equanimity, rather than avoiding the world.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Sariputta's bright face, and your line, review the road. What rose on the way when you walked it back? Today, the last of the hundred and fifty-two. Day five hundred seventeen.

The last discourse in the Middle-Length Sayings opens with a short, slightly awkward conversation. The Buddha is staying at Kajangala, and a young brahmin named Uttara comes to visit. He's a student of a teacher called Parasariya. Does your teacher teach the development of the senses? the Buddha asks. Yes, says Uttara. How? Like this: you don't see forms with the eye, and you don't hear sounds with the ear. Then, the Buddha says, a blind person and a deaf person must be very developed indeed. Today: seeing, not swept.
screen: `THE LAST DISCOURSE.` → `UTTARA'S TEACHER: DON'T SEE.` → `THEN THE BLIND ARE DEVELOPED?`

segments.voice: Uttara goes quiet. The text says he sat silent, shoulders drooping, head down, with nothing to say. The Buddha doesn't press him. He turns to Ananda and teaches the other way, the development of the senses in his own discipline. When someone sees a form with the eye, something agreeable arises, or disagreeable, or both. That's going to happen. Eyes see. The trained person understands: this has arisen in me. It's conditioned, it's coarse, it's dependently arisen. But there's something peaceful and fine: equanimity. Then the reaction fades, and equanimity remains. The pictures are about speed. For the eye, as quickly as someone with good sight might open and shut their eyes. For the ear, as quickly as a strong man snaps his fingers. For the nose, like raindrops rolling off a sloping lotus leaf without sticking. For the tongue, like spitting out a bit of saliva gathered on the tip of the tongue. For the body, like a strong man straightening a bent arm. For the mind, like two or three drops of water falling on an iron pan heated all day: they vanish almost at once. The Pali word for the senses here is indriya, the faculties. So the last discourse of the whole collection lands on something modest. Training isn't shutting the senses down. Liking and disliking will still arise. The skill is in what happens next: seeing it, and letting it go before it carries you off. The eyes stay open. You see, and you stay.
screen: `UTTARA, SILENT, SHOULDERS DOWN` · `THIS HAS ARISEN IN ME` · `A BLINK, A SNAP, A DROP ON IRON` · `EYES OPEN, NOT CARRIED OFF` · then, large: `SEE AND STAY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: see without being swept. Let your gaze rest, eyes open and soft, on whatever is in front of you. When a liking or a disliking rises, a little pull or push, notice it: this has arisen. Then let it fall away, like water on a hot pan. Back to just seeing. If a thought drags you off, that's fine. Open and shut your eyes once, and begin again. The bell holds the time.
Seeing. Not closing the eyes, but seeing what arises, liking or disliking, and letting it settle into equanimity before it sweeps you away. Today's word.
Your line: see and stay. Today, when something you dislike comes into view, keep looking, notice the push, and let it pass like a blink. Day five hundred seventeen.

screen: `DAY 517 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: LOOKING BACK: THE GOOD POTTER.`

options: turns to Ananda and teaches the other way.

fork.reveal: he lets the silence stand and teaches Ananda the noble development of the senses, with Uttara still sitting there to hear it.

original.note: Pali and Sanskrit indriya: faculty, sense power. MN 152 is about developing all six.

trapdoor: what you thought: training the senses means shutting them down.
what it means: seeing what arises, liking or disliking, and letting it settle into equanimity, quickly.

what a scholar hears: the Indriyabhavana Sutta closes the Majjhima with a graded teaching (the noble development, the learner, the noble one) and six similes whose common thread is the speed of letting go.

sources.ref: Majjhima Nikaya 152, Indriyabhavana Sutta (the development of the faculties)

518.title: Looking back: the good potter
518.hook: a discourse we passed: the potter Ghatikara, who cared for his blind parents and kept the precepts
518.howItsDone: Buddhist teaching across schools holds up care for parents as a great merit, and lay followers like Ghatikara are remembered as models of a householder's practice: refuge, precepts, honest livelihood and generosity.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the last discourse, and the word seeing. Your line was see and stay. Did something you disliked pass like a blink? Today ends a week, and we step back to a discourse we walked past. Day five hundred eighteen.

The Buddha is walking through Kosala with his monks when he stops at a certain spot by the road and smiles. Ananda knows a Buddha doesn't smile without a reason, so he asks. Long ago, the Buddha says, there was a market town right here, and in it lived a potter named Ghatikara. That's the eighty-first discourse, which we passed on our way through the collection. It's the story of a man with clay on his hands, and no robe, who the text holds up as a model. Today, looking back: the good potter.
screen: `THE BUDDHA SMILES BY THE ROAD.` → `A TOWN WAS HERE, LONG AGO.` → `A POTTER NAMED GHATIKARA.`

segments.voice: In the story, Ghatikara lives in the time of an earlier Buddha, Kassapa, and he's that Buddha's chief lay supporter. His best friend is a young brahmin named Jotipala, who doesn't want to go see some shaven-headed recluse. Ghatikara drags him by the belt, and then, astonishingly, by the hair. A potter grabbing a brahmin by the hair! Jotipala decides something serious must be going on, goes, listens, and becomes a monk. The text says that Jotipala was the Buddha himself, long before. So the potter is the friend who got the future Buddha to his first teacher. But the heart of the story is how Ghatikara lives. He keeps the precepts. He's gone for refuge. He won't dig the ground himself, so he makes pots only from clay at broken riverbanks or heaps left by rats. He doesn't haggle: he sets his pots out and tells people to leave some rice or beans and take what they need. And he looks after his parents, who are old and blind. Once, while he's away, Kassapa Buddha comes for alms, finds no one home, and helps himself to rice from the pot. The blind parents are delighted when they hear. Another time Kassapa's hut leaks in the rains, and his monks take the grass from Ghatikara's own roof to fix it. His parents say: take it. The text says his roofless house stayed dry for three months. So a householder, not a monk, is the hero. Care for elders, honest trade and steady virtue, done with your hands.
screen: `THE FRIEND DRAGGED BY THE HAIR` · `CLAY FROM BROKEN RIVERBANKS` · `BLIND PARENTS, CARED FOR` · `THE ROOF GIVEN AWAY` · then, large: `THE GOOD POTTER.`

segments.voice: First, look back at this week: Rahula under the tree, all of it changing. Six sets of six. Not inflamed. Who to respect. Review the road. See and stay. Now the practice: care for an elder today. Bring to mind an older person in your life. A parent, a neighbor, someone frail. Picture their face. Breathe in their wellbeing, and decide on one small thing: a call, a visit, a chore done for them. The bell holds the time.
Looking back. Returning to a discourse we passed, and finding a quiet hero: a potter who cared for his parents and kept the precepts. Today's word.
Your line: the good potter. Today, do one ordinary task with honest hands, the way Ghatikara made pots, and offer one kindness to an elder. Day five hundred eighteen.

fork.setup: you're Ghatikara's old, blind parents. your son is away, and monks come asking for the grass from your roof to fix their teacher's leaking hut. what do you say?
options: take it.
wait until our son comes home.
take only half.
fork.reveal: they say take it, and the text says the roofless house stayed dry for the three months of rain.

original.note: Pali and Sanskrit upasaka: a lay follower, one who sits near. Ghatikara is the model upasaka.

trapdoor: what you thought: in the early texts the heroes are always monks.
what it means: in MN 81 the hero is a potter who cares for his blind parents and keeps the precepts.

what a scholar hears: the Ghatikara Sutta is one of the few discourses set in a past Buddha's time, told because the Buddha remembers a place; Ghatikara is called a non-returner, a lay person at the third stage of awakening.

sources.ref: Majjhima Nikaya 81, Ghatikara Sutta (the potter Ghatikara)
